title: As an offering
hook: whatever you do, eat, give, do it as an offering (Bhagavad Gita 9.27)

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was svadharma: better your own duty, done imperfectly, than another's done well. Your line was imperfect, and our own.

A leaf. A flower. A piece of fruit. A little water. In the ninth chapter of the Bhagavad Gita, Krishna names these small things and says that when they're offered with devotion, he accepts them. Nothing on the list is costly. And then, a verse later, Krishna widens it past anything that could fit on a plate. Not only leaves and flowers. Everything. Today's word is what happens when the whole working day becomes the plate.
screen: `A LEAF, A FLOWER, FRUIT, WATER.` → `OFFERED WITH DEVOTION.` → `THEN, EVERYTHING.`

segments.voice: Here's the verse, in paraphrase: whatever you do, whatever you eat, whatever you offer in worship, whatever you give away, whatever discipline you practice, do it as an offering to me. First, notice the list. It starts with doing, and eating comes second. Not prayer, not ritual: the ordinary verbs of a day come first. The Sanskrit word for this kind of offering is arpana, something handed over, given up to God. Second, what changes. The work itself might not change at all: the same report, the same pot of rice, the same shift. What changes is who it's for. In the Gita, a deed done as an offering isn't done mainly for praise, or pay, or even for the result. The next verse says that by doing this a person is freed from the bonds that actions bring, good or bad. Third, who is speaking. In the Gita, Krishna speaks as God. Hindus who worship Krishna hear the verse as a direct invitation to give him everything. Readers from other Hindu schools understand the 'me' in their own ways, and commentators have read the Gita from different directions. Fourth, where the verse lands. A nurse taking a pulse. A student writing an essay at midnight. Someone folding laundry for a family that won't say thanks. In the Gita's picture, any of these can be laid down like a flower, not because the task is grand, but because of how it's handed over. A leaf is enough. So is one task, done and given away.
screen: `WHATEVER YOU DO, EAT, GIVE.` · `THE SAME TASK, A NEW ADDRESS.` · `KRISHNA SPEAKS AS GOD.` · `A TASK LAID DOWN LIKE A FLOWER.` · then, large: `DO IT AS AN OFFERING.`

segments.voice: Pick one ordinary task waiting for you today, a meal, a message, a repair, and picture yourself doing it slowly and well. Then picture handing it over when it's done, the way you'd set a flower down, to God if that's your way, or to the people it serves, or simply to the day, breathing in as you hold it and out as you let it go. If you pray, you can offer it in your own tradition's words.
Arpana. The Gita's word for an offering: whatever you do, eat or give, handed over to God. Today's word.
Your line: laid down like a flower. The same task, a new address. Day eight hundred ninety-three, done.
